en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui, Part Two:
Verification of the Whirling Senses Returning to Their Nature. Section Five: One, Aniruddha. Subsection Three: One, Narrating the Causes and Conditions for Awakening.
Aniruddha then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When I first left the home life, I was constantly fond of sleep; the Tathāgata rebuked me, calling me a member of the animal realm.”
Upon hearing the Buddha’s rebuke, I wept and reproached myself; for seven days I did not sleep, and consequently lost both my eyes.
The World-Honored One then revealed to me the Vajra Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Illuminating Radiance.

Alternatively, Aniruddha is rendered as A-ni-lou-dou or Cheng-a-nou-lou-da; these are slight variations of the Sanskrit sound, translated here as "Unextinguished" (Wumie) or "As One Wishes" (Ruyi). He was the younger brother of the Buddha's maternal uncle and the son of Śuklodana.
The Tathāgata rebuked those who take great pleasure in sleep, saying:
"Alas! Alas!
Why do you sleep like snails, conchs, clams, and oysters? Having slept for a thousand years, you shall not hear the name of the Buddha."
Therefore, it is said that he rebuked the class of animals.

While it was commonly said that he possessed "half-a-head" divine vision (*divyacakṣus*), here it is called the "Vajra Samādhi"; this reveals actual realization and differs from what was previously stated, which should be understood through the meaning.
2. Second, the formal presentation of the realization of the ultimate meaning:

"I do not rely on the eyes to perceive the ten directions; my essential truth is transparently clear, like looking at a fruit in the palm of my hand. Thus, the Tathāgata has certified me as an Arhat."
The function manifested by the Vajra-samādhi is identical to the Buddha’s vision and function; therefore, it is said that "the refined and true penetrates clearly, seeing the ten directions.
Third, this concludes the response to the question.
"The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; according to what I have realized, to revolve the seeing and follow the source is the foremost method.

By revolving that deluded seeing and following that true source, the perception of objects is extinguished and the refined reality shines forth clearly. When all things are unimpeded, how could it be limited merely to subtle forms beyond obstructions?"
2. Cūḍapanthaka: Three sections.
First, an account of his background.
Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I lack the capacity for recitation and upholding; I am not of a nature for extensive learning.

Having first encountered a Buddha and heard the Dharma, I went forth from the household life; yet, though I could remember a single gāthā of the Tathāgata, for a hundred days I was unable to retain what came before while losing what came after, or retain what came after while losing what came before.”
The Buddha, pitying my folly, instructed me to dwell in retreat and regulate my inhalation and exhalation.
Cūḍapanthaka—also known as Sarpadāsa, meaning "Born on the Road," or alternatively called "Successor of the Path"—was so named because he was born by the side of a road.

By nature he was dull-witted; in the past he had been a great Dharma master who was well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras and had five hundred disciples. Yet, out of secret stinginess, he was unwilling to teach the Buddha-dharma to others. Consequently, in his later life, he was born with dark ignorance. Due to the roots of goodness from his former lives, he encountered the Buddha and left the household life; however, when five hundred bhikṣus taught him a single verse together, he could not master it even after ninety days.
To remedy distraction, he was taught the practice of counting the breaths.
Second, the formal presentation of his realization of the ultimate meaning:

"At that time, as I contemplated the breath until its subtlest limits were exhausted, I perceived the moments (*kṣaṇa*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. My mind suddenly opened up and attained great unimpededness; eventually, with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), I became an Arhat, sat beneath the Buddha’s seat, and was certified as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)."
First, one contemplates the wind of the breath as arising and ceasing from moment to moment, until its subtlest aspects are exhausted and its arising and ceasing are found to have no source.

Once the wind of the breath is empty and the mind is free from discrimination, there is a sudden and great awakening to the fact that all things are without obstruction; this not only counteracts distraction, but also reveals the true mark of the breath.
3. Conclusion and Response to the Inquiry:
"Regarding the Buddha’s question on perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, returning the breath to follow emptiness is the foremost method.
By reversing the breath of birth-and-death and following the emptiness of non-arising, one illuminates through the breath; this is the unsurpassed way."
3. Gavāmpati: Three sections.
First, the account of the cause for his realization.
Gavāmpati immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I had karmic offenses of speech; during past kalpas, I mocked śramaṇas, and thus in life after life I have suffered from the ailment of rumination.
The Tathāgata has shown me the Dharma-gate of the single-flavor pure mind-ground, through which I have attained the cessation of the mind and entered samādhi.”
It is also called *guptapātra*, which in this language means "ox-chewer" (*gomayakhādaka*).
Just as an ox often makes a hollow sound even when not eating, the mouth of this person resembles the snorting of an ox.

The *Mahāśāstra* provides a different account of its origins than the sutra; it teaches that by contemplating the faculty of the tongue and tasting flavors, one enters the Way and shall attain the Dharma-gate of the single flavor of the mind-ground.
The cognition that perceives flavors is extinguished forever from this point on; therefore, it is said that he "extinguishes the mind and enters samādhi.
Second, the formal presentation of the realization of the ultimate meaning, in two parts:
first, the description of the contemplative practice.
"Observe that the cognition of taste is neither the substance nor the object; by reflecting thus, one may transcend all worldly outflows (*āsrava*).
Observe this faculty of tasting: it does not arise from its own substance, nor does it arise from another object. Since each is individually without arising, how could they possibly exist together?"
Neither found within conditions nor existing apart from them, from where could the cognition that perceives flavors ultimately arise?
As it is with one faculty, so it is with all faculties; by contemplating this, one should transcend all outflows.
2. Description of the Benefits of Contemplation:

"Internally liberated from body and mind, externally transcending the world, and far removed from the three realms of existence, he is like a bird escaping its cage. With defilements stripped away and dust extinguished, his Dharma-eye becomes pure and he attains Arhatship; the Tathāgata personally confirms him as having ascended the path of No-more-learning."
The faculties having returned to their source, one is liberated from within; the sense objects having dissolved, one is cast off from without.
Since both internal and external have vanished, who is there to dwell in the three realms of existence?
Therefore, it is called "detachment."

Perception (*saṃjñā*) and its characteristics are the dust, and the conscious mind (*vijñāna*) is the defilement; when both are left far behind, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and thus it is said that the Dharma-eye is pure.
Third, this concludes the answer to the question.
"When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the Way, according to what I have realized, returning to the flavor and revolving the faculty of cognition is the foremost.
To revolve the deluded faculties and sense-objects and return to the true reality is to have the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground revealed all at once; this is the foremost.
4. Pīṅgala-batṣa: Three sections.
First, the account of the cause for his awakening.
Pīṅgala-batṣa immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since I first resolved to attain enlightenment and entered the Path under the Buddha, I have frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of the many things in the world that are not to be enjoyed.
While begging for alms in the city, my mind was contemplating these Dharma gates; I did not notice that a poisonous thorn had pierced my foot on the road, causing my entire body to ache with pain."
Piliṅgavatsa said it was due to "residual habits.
His calling the goddess of the Ganges a "little slave" was not out of intentional malice, but rather resulted from the residual habit of pride he had as a brahmin in past lives.

When he first entered the Path, he heard the Buddha teach that the world is suffering, empty, impermanent, and impure, and that it is entirely devoid of delight; subsequently, while practicing alms-gathering, he contemplated entering this meditative observation, when he suddenly encountered a painful circumstance, hence the mention of his "pain."
2. The formal presentation of the realization of the principle, in two parts:
A. Narrating the contemplative practice:
"I reflect that there is knowing; this knowing perceives this profound suffering. Although the awareness perceives the pain, the pure mind of awareness is free from any perception of pain."
I further reflected:
"In such a single body, how could there possibly be two separate cognitions?
This refers to mindfulness, which is contemplation.
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is awareness.
One gives rise to contemplation based on sensation (*vedanā*), contemplating that this body of mine possesses knowledge and awareness that perceives this deep pain.

Although one gives rise to this contemplation, observing both awareness and sensation, one contemplates the pure mind which has neither pain nor awareness. These faculties, objects, and discursive thoughts exist within the deluded body-mind, but do not exist within the truly pure mind.
Furthermore, when one further observes the perception of painful sensation and the awareness of a pure mind, these constitute two distinct perceptions. From what do they arise?

If there were two perceptions within a single body, it would follow that there should be two Buddhas; therefore, one knows that these perceptions are entirely illusory, and within the pure mind, nothing at all can be apprehended.
2. Clarifying the Attainment of Enlightenment:

"Not long after he had focused his mindfulness, his body and mind suddenly became empty. Within twenty-one days, all outflows were exhausted, and he became an Arhat. He received the seal of personal certification and realized the state of No-more-learning."
When the thought of grasping at anything does not arise for even a single moment, it is called "gathering" (samādhi).

At that juncture, the grasper and the grasped, the observer and the observed, all simultaneously become quiescent; non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) immediately manifests, and one realizes the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); hence it is said that body and mind suddenly become empty.
Third, the conclusion answering the question:
"Regarding the Buddha’s inquiry into perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, 'pure awareness leaving the body behind' is the foremost.

Since both the subject that observes and the object observed, as well as the sensation and the one who feels it, are quiescent and non-existent as even a single dharma, it is called "pure awareness leaving the body behind."
5. Subhūti, Part Three:
First, recounting his past realization.
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since beginningless kalpas, my mind has attained non-obstruction; I recall my births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
From the very moment I was first in my mother’s womb, I already knew emptiness and stillness.

Subhūti, he is called Śūnyatā-utpanna (Born of Emptiness), also known as Supratiṣṭhita (Well-Established) and others, because at the time of his birth he manifested emptiness, his mind penetrated emptiness, and he constantly cultivated practices of emptiness; therefore, these were his names.
Since it is said that [this has been so] for kalpas as vast as the sands of the Ganges, one knows that it is empty and quiescent; how could it be that realization was attained only today?
Second, clarifying the realization of the essential meaning, in two parts:
first, realizing mere emptiness.
"In this way, even until the ten directions become empty, one also causes sentient beings to realize emptiness.

By practicing the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one understands that the mind is empty and quiescent; thus, all environments and inhabitants, self and others, the defiled and the pure, and even everything throughout the ten directions that arises through the transformation of the mind, all become empty.
Having realized this for oneself, one also causes others to realize emptiness.
Because this exclusively empty [state] is not yet fully endowed with all phenomena, it is called "mere emptiness.
Second, realizing emptiness within emptiness.

"Having received the Tathāgata’s instruction on awakening to the true emptiness of one's nature, and through the perfect clarity of that empty nature, I attained arhatship. I suddenly entered the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness, shared in the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and was certified as one beyond training; thus, through liberation in the emptiness of nature, I have become supreme."
The realization of the intrinsic nature as true emptiness is the principle of the Middle Way.

Because this emptiness is the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is fully pervasive and endowed with all dharmas; for its luminosity universally illumines the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. Like a *maṇi* jewel that produces things according to one’s wishes, and like the great deep and vast ocean that contains and encompasses all, the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) penetrates, understands, and illuminates such that object and wisdom are of one essence—this is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Although one realizes emptiness, one is not bound by emptiness; therefore, it is called liberation.
Third, the conclusion answering this question:

"The Buddha asks about perfect penetration: according to what I have realized, all phenomena enter into non-existence, and that which is 'non' is itself exhausted; turning back from phenomena to return to nothingness—this is the foremost."
Initially, one uses single emptiness to empty all marks, hence it is said "entering non-existence.
Next, one uses double emptiness to empty the mark of emptiness itself, hence it is said "non-exhaustion," wherein even non-existence is empty.
The above five persons have completed their entry into realization according to their faculties.
Third, the realization of the tranquil consciousness by tracing its source, which has six parts;
first, Śāriputra, which has three parts:
1. Narrating Past Realization.
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For kalpas as vast as the sands of the Ganges, my mind and vision have been pure, and I have undergone such births as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.”
"Various transformations of both the mundane and supramundane worlds are understood at a single glance, and one attains non-obstruction.
Śāriputra—also called Śakraputra or Śarīraputra.

When the mind’s vision is pure, it means that visual consciousness gives rise to wisdom, perceiving all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds, thoroughly penetrating their fundamental causes and conditions; this constitutes the attainment of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Discerning all phenomena is called the Dharma-eye.
Second, clarifying present awakening has two parts:
first, obtaining the wisdom-eye.
"I encountered the Kāśyapa brothers on the road as they were traveling together; through their discourse on causes and conditions, I realized that the mind is boundless.
The Kāśyapa brothers referred to here are the Three Kāśyapas.
The proclamation of causes and conditions is precisely the Dharma of the Three Truths.

Through the teaching of the causes, understanding arises; by awakening to the principle of true emptiness, one attains the realization of the first fruit, which is the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

As for other places where it is said that he encountered Aśvajit, this may refer to those encountered at the same time rather than to a single individual alone; the sūtras merely cite them interchangeably.

Having heard the principle of dependent origination, one realizes that dependent origination is itself empty; thus, one attains the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) and perceives the truth of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).
Second, one attains the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*).

Having left the household life following the Buddha, one perceives the perfect clarity of awakening, attains great fearlessness, and becomes an Arhat. As the eldest son of the Buddha, one is born from the Buddha’s mouth and born through transformation by the Dharma.
When the clarity of seeing and awareness becomes perfectly full, it is the true awakening’s wondrous clarity, fully accomplished and manifested through the visual consciousness.
This is because the Tathāgata revealed the sublime Dharma, enabling me to attain realization; therefore, it is said to proceed from his mouth and from the Dharma.
3. Conclusion and Response to the Question:

"Regarding the Buddha’s inquiry into perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the mind and vision emit light, and when this light reaches its ultimate limit, it becomes knowing-seeing; this is the foremost."

From the visual consciousness, the light of wisdom is manifested; the ultimate limit of this light of wisdom is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. It is the simultaneous perfection of the three knowledges and the five eyes, and is therefore called "ultimate."
2. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, in three parts:
1. Undertaking Practice by Serving the Buddha.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have already served as a Dharma Prince for Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; when the Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct their disciples whose faculties are those of Bodhisattvas to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra, they derive my name from me."
His practice pervades the entire Dharma-realm, hence he is called "Universal" (Puxian); his rank is adjacent to that of the Ultimate Sage, hence he is called "Worthy" (Xian).
Among the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he serves as a Dharma Prince; all disciples of the Buddhas who have resolved to practice this path are named Samantabhadra.
2. The Accomplishment of Practice and the Arising of Function, in two parts:
1. Pointing to the Essence and Briefly Indicating.
"World-Honored One!..."
"I use my mind to hear and distinguish all the knowledge and views of sentient beings.
"Hearing with the mind" refers to the manifestation of the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*).

From this ear-consciousness, one attains true perfect penetration and enters the principle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); birth-and-death consciousness ceases, and quiescent extinction manifests before one. When object and wisdom merge in mutual obscurity, they become a single entity without duality; thus, one returns to the hearing of the mind to initiate its function, distinguishing the knowledge and views of sentient beings, and manifests their bodies for those who can be enlightened.
2. Extensive Explanation According to Capabilities:

"If, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, there is a single sentient being who brings forth the realization of Samantabhadra’s practice within their mind, at that time I shall mount the six-tusked elephant, manifesting hundreds of thousands of bodies, and arrive at that very place."

"Even if their hindrances are so deep that they have not yet attained the sight of me, I shall, in the midst of darkness, touch the crown of their heads, protect and comfort them, and cause them to achieve success.

Since the hearing by means of the mind accords with the essence of the Dharma-realm, and object and wisdom are non-dual, there is nothing among all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm whose minds do not clearly perceive the practitioner of Samantabhadra, nor is there any response that is not initiated; thus, both those who respond to the teachings through the hidden and the manifest attain their benefit.
3. Conclusion and Response to the Question:
"The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; I have explained its fundamental cause. When the hearing of the mind is illuminated and discernment becomes sovereign, this is the foremost."
As in the text.
Third, Sundarananda, in three parts:
first, the account of receiving the Honored One’s instruction.
Sundarananda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When I first left the household life and entered the Way under the Buddha, although I was fully endowed with the precepts, my mind was constantly distracted and unstable during samādhi, and I had not yet attained the state beyond outflows.”
"The World-Honored One has instructed me and Kūṭadanta to contemplate the white [spot] at the tip of the nose.
Sundarananda—here translated as "Glorious Joy"—was so named after his wife; he was the Buddha’s own younger brother.

Previously, when practicing counting the breaths, it was explained in terms of the sense faculties; now, it is explained in terms of observing consciousness. One fixes the mind by focusing on the white [light] at the tip of the nose, so that it does not become distracted or disturbed.
Second, cultivating the contemplation according to the instructions, which has two parts:
first, clarifying the practice of contemplation.

"I first observed with true discernment for twenty-one days, seeing the breath entering and exiting my nostrils like smoke; my body and mind became inwardly luminous, and the world became a transparent void, everywhere pure and clear, like lapis lazuli."
"As the appearance of smoke gradually fades, the breath becomes white.
Initially observing the white appearance, after three weeks have passed, one sees the vital breath as being like the appearance of smoke.

When this contemplation is perfected, it issues forth from within the body and mind; whether it be the body or the environment, all at once become empty and pure, with inner and outer reflecting each other through transparency, like lapis lazuli.

This is because, by contemplating the cessation of the signs of arising and ceasing, the observing mind becomes fused and luminous; as the wisdom of emptiness is about to arise, one consequently penetrates the realms of the body.
Yet, as this is still within the stage of skillful means and one has not yet been able to forget objective conditions, one perceives that the smoke transforms into a white sign.
2. Clarifying the benefit of awakening:
"The mind opened and outflows were exhausted; all inhalations and exhalations were transformed into radiance, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions, and he attained arhatship."
"The World-Honored One has prophesied that I shall attain Bodhi.

Since the wisdom of non-arising emptiness has already manifested before me, all breaths do not arise and consist purely of wisdom; the radiance of this wisdom illuminates all things as they truly are, such that the worlds and sentient beings are none other than perfect and wondrous. By means of this, my outflows are exhausted and I shall attain Bodhi.
3. Conclusion and Response to the Question: "The Buddha asks about perfect penetration;
I have attained it through the cessation of mental activity. Through long-term cessation, clarity was revealed; with this perfected clarity, outflows were extinguished. This is the foremost method."

As in the text. Fourth, Pūrṇa, in three parts: first, recounting his past eloquence, in two parts: [1] the actual recounting; [2] the conclusion. (The first part follows: "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra... and so on, as in the text. Second, the Buddha’s praise. Third, the assembly’s rejoicing. Fifth, Śāriputra, in three parts: first, the Buddha’s instruction; second, Śāriputra’s inquiry; third, the Buddha’s answer. 1. Fully Discussing the Provisional and the Real.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For kalpas as vast as space, my eloquence has been unimpeded; I have proclaimed suffering and emptiness, and have deeply penetrated the true reality.”
"Pūrṇa" means "full. "Maitrāyaṇī" means "compassion," with "nī" being a feminine suffix.
He has attained the four types of analytical eloquence; this has been so for vast eons, not merely today.

The true reality of suffering and emptiness is precisely the dharma of the provisional and the real. For countless kalpas, he has inwardly concealed his true nature while outwardly manifesting in various forms to bring sentient beings to maturity. Thus it has been throughout successive ages.
Second, the Exposition of Dharma Gates:
"In this manner, even regarding the secret dharma gates of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have revealed them subtly within the assembly, attaining fearlessness."

"This is not merely the Dharma-gate taught by a single Buddha; rather, regarding the secret teachings heard from Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I proclaim them all for the sake of the assembly with fearlessness.
To say they are 'subtle and wondrous' means that one skillfully employs words, parables, and expedient means to accord with the capacities and responses of sentient beings."
2. Manifest Realization:

"The World-Honored One knew that I possessed great eloquence, and so He instructed me with the wheel of His voice to proclaim it forth. In the presence of the Buddha, I assisted the Buddha in turning the wheel; through this lion’s roar, I attained arhatship."
“The World-Honored One has certified my teaching of the Dharma as unsurpassed.

Knowing that I possessed the talent and wisdom for eloquence, the Tathāgata subsequently instructed me to teach the Dharma by means of the wheel of speech. This was to demonstrate that one should not employ a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to expound the Dharma of true reality (dharmatā). Therefore, as the purity of the Dharma taught follows, so too is there purity of wisdom; as the purity of wisdom follows, so too is there purity of mind.
The "Lion’s Roar" refers to speaking with fearlessness.
Third, the conclusion that responds to the question:
"When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, I rely on the sound of the Dharma to subdue demonic adversaries and extinguish all outflows; this is the foremost."

Internally, by means of meditative concentration and wisdom, one subdues and severs craving and false views; externally, by means of supernormal powers and the preaching of the Dharma, one subjugates Māra and non-Buddhists. Thus, the city of Nirvāṇa endures, and the Three Jewels are never interrupted.
5. Upāli, three [sections]:
First, meeting the Buddha and receiving his teaching.
Upāli immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I personally followed the Buddha when he left the city to renounce the world; I personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity; and I personally saw the Tathāgata subdue all Māras, restrain all non-Buddhists, and liberate the world from the outflows of greed and desire."

"Having received the Buddha's instruction on the precepts," Upāli said, "The term 'near-attendant' (*upasthāyaka*) refers to the minister who served as a close attendant when the Tathāgata was a prince.

Just as he attended to him in his lay life, so too did he do so after his renunciation; thus he witnessed the practice of subduing Māra and repelling outsiders, severing delusions, and attaining the Way."

Therefore, upholding the precepts by following the Tathāgata’s teaching, he disciplined the Śākya clan within the Vinaya; as for his having ordained Upāli first, it was because although Upāli had followed the Buddha at the outset, he was only then able to receive ordination.
2. Realization through Precepts:

"In this way, even unto the three thousand modes of deportment and the eighty thousand subtle categories of natural and proscribed offenses, all are completely purified; body and mind are stilled and extinguished, and one becomes an Arhat."

"I am the pillar of discipline within the assembly of the Tathāgata; my mind has been personally sealed by him. Upholding the precepts and cultivating the body, I am esteemed as foremost by the multitude.

I possess a majestic presence that inspires awe and a dignified demeanor worthy of emulation. Each of the two hundred and fifty precepts has four modes of conduct, and when these are further correlated with the three clusters [of offenses], they total three thousand."

Furthermore, by assigning three thousand to each of the seven branches of body and speech and dividing them according to the four categories of afflictions, they are transformed into eighty-four thousand; this present figure is merely a general enumeration.

Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are inherently sinful by their very nature; they do not depend on external prohibition, for their commission immediately constitutes karma. Therefore, they are called "inherent karma" (*prakṛti-karma*).

The remaining [offenses] were established as prohibitions only after faults had arisen; prior to their establishment, committing them constituted no offense, and thus they are called "prohibitive actions" (*vārita-karman*).

Because one maintains the precepts, one does not transgress against various sensory objects (*viṣaya*); since these objects do not arise, the body is likewise not acquired, and thus the body is quiescent (*śānta*).
If my body does not exist, upon what can my mind rely?
Since the sense organs and their objects have both vanished, the mind has nothing to possess and is therefore also in a state of quiescent extinction.
Thus, all phenomena are simultaneously pure; this single, precious awakening is fundamentally undefiled—this is true upholding of the precepts—and it is through this that realization is attained.

What is called the "governing framework" refers to the essential points by which one can discern the gravity of offenses, determine what is permitted or prohibited, and distinguish between upholding and violating the precepts; it regulates the conduct of the assembly and ensures that the person and the Dharma are held in high esteem as a model for future generations.
3. Conclusion and Response to the Question:
“When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I attained mastery over the body by focusing on it;
subsequently, I focused on the mind and attained thorough penetration of the mind.”
Thereafter, body and mind will become entirely supple and functional; this is the foremost state.

By upholding the precepts and cultivating the person, one restrains and prevents defilement. When one contemplates the true mark of the body, defilements do not arise of themselves; one realizes that the discriminating mind has no basis upon which it can exist. Therefore, body and mind attain unimpeded mastery and freedom.
6. Maudgalyāyana, three parts:
First, hearing the teaching upon encountering circumstances.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first went out on the road to beg for alms, I encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers—Uruvilvā, Gayā, and Nadī—and expounded to them the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causes and conditions."
Maudgalyāyana is his clan name; "Maudgalya" means "Bean-gatherer.
Kolita is his personal name; "Kolita" means "Knotless Tree.
Uruvilvā refers to the "Wood-apple Grove."
Gayā means "City"; Nadi means "River.
This is based on the *Śāriputra-madhyama-saṃnipāta-sūtra*.
2. Attaining Enlightenment through the Universal Teaching of Causes; Part Two:
1. Attaining Awakening and Entering the Path.
"I suddenly gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and attained great, pervasive penetration."
"The Tathāgata has bestowed this kāṣāya upon me to wear, and my beard and hair have fallen away of their own accord.
Having heard these profound meanings of the causes and conditions, he immediately, through those very causes and conditions, deeply penetrated the true nature of reality (dharmatā).
The true mark is signless; body and mind are quiescent. Through this, one attains awakening, which is called "Great Penetration.
Second, one attains penetration through awakening:
"I travel throughout the ten directions without obstruction; my supernormal powers are so brilliant that they are ranked as unsurpassed, and I have become an Arhat."
"Not only does the World-Honored One do so, but the Tathāgatas of the ten directions also praise my spiritual power as perfectly bright and pure, sovereign and fearless.

This means that by awakening to the fact that discrimination does not arise and the mental consciousness does not stir, one uses this profound stillness to revolve the false and extinguish birth, thereby subduing the mind and returning to original enlightenment.

Since the profound nature is deep and the light of the mind is fully manifested, the great functioning of supernormal powers appears before one; thus, one is able to travel through the ten directions with unimpeded mastery.
Third, the conclusion that responds by reiterating the core point.

“The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; I attained it by returning to the stillness of the ocean of consciousness, whereby the light of the mind was released and proclaimed, like a turbid stream that becomes clear and crystalline after a long time—this is my foremost method.”
The swirling stillness is itself concentration; the radiance of the mind is itself wisdom.
From concentration arises wisdom, whose divine function is boundless, like clear water in which all myriad forms appear.
The above six persons have completed their entry into awakening by means of consciousness.
Fourth, they further largely accord with fundamental realization, in seven parts:
first, Vajra Fire-Head, in three parts:
1. Encountering the Buddha and Hearing His Teaching.
Before the Tathāgata, Ucchuṣma joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I constantly recall that in the distant past, for many kalpas, my nature was characterized by much greed and desire.”
There was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Śūnyarāja, who taught that those with excessive lust become a mass of fierce fire.
Ucchuṣma— here translated as "Fire-Head"—
due to his great greed, heard this teaching and practiced contemplation, thereby attaining awakening.

Those in whom greed is rampant possess the cause for the hell of ghosts; as the cause is inflamed by the fire of desire, the effect is scorched by the fire of karma—cause and effect being commensurate, both are termed "masses of fire."
2. Cultivating Contemplation Based on the Teaching, in two parts:
A. Attaining Enlightenment through the Completion of Contemplation.

"Teach me to observe throughout the hundred skeletal members and four limbs all sensations of cold and warmth. As the spiritual light coalesces within, it transforms my excessive lustful mind into the fire of wisdom."
"First I observed my body and mind and saw only the sensation of warmth; later, observing that warm breath, it was without characteristic and without arising.
My own body is itself empty—upon what, then, could warmth depend to abide?"
When body and mind have become tranquil, the subtle fire of one’s nature manifests; thus it is said that the divine light coalesces within to form the fire of wisdom.
Second, a further explanation is provided to establish this:
"From then on, all Buddhas called me by the name 'Fire-Head' (Agnimukha)."
By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, I attained Arhatship and made this great vow:
"When all Buddhas attain the Way, may I become a mighty warrior to personally subdue their demonic adversaries."
"By contemplating the nature of fire, he attained the true samādhi; because he took fire as the initial gateway for entering the Way, he is called 'Fire-Head' (Huotou).
Since fire can destroy all dharmas, he made a great vow to take the body of a powerful warrior (mahābala) to shatter Māra and protect the Dharma."
3. Conclusion and Response to the Inquiry:

"When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, I have observed through contemplation that the warmth and touch of my body and mind flow unimpededly; once all outflows were extinguished, a great jewel-flame arose, and I attained supreme enlightenment—this is the foremost method."
The sensation of warmth is itself emptiness; therefore, it is called "unimpeded.
The nature of fire wondrously manifests; therefore, it is called "circulating.
It coagulates within and appears without; therefore, precious flames are produced.
II. Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara: three sections. A.
Meeting the Buddha and receiving his teachings: two sections. 1.
Generally encountering various Buddhas and fully cultivating meritorious deeds.
The Bodhisattva Earth-Holder rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I recall that in the past, when the Tathāgata Universal Radiance appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu. Whenever there were irregularities on all major roads, ferry crossings, fields, or narrow passes that caused damage or obstruction to carts and horses, I would level and fill them; I would either construct bridges or carry sand and earth to do so.”

Thus, through diligent toil, I have passed through the appearance of immeasurable Buddhas in the world. There may be sentient beings in the marketplace who require someone to carry their goods; I first carry them for them, and once we reach their destination, I set down the goods and depart, taking no payment.
"Exerting his body and toiling himself for the benefit of the many, he has practiced the gift of fearlessness under immeasurable Buddhas; thus his roots of merit are vast.
A market enclosure is called *huán*, and a market gate is called *huì*."
2. Specifically meeting Viśvabhū Buddha and receiving his instruction:

"When the Buddha Viśvabhū was present in the world, there was widespread famine. At that time, I was a porter; whether the distance was far or near, I would accept only one coin. If a cart or ox became mired in the mud, I possessed supernatural power and would push its wheels for them, thereby relieving their suffering."

At that time, the Great King of the country invited the Buddha to a vegetarian feast. I leveled the ground at that moment to await the Buddha, whereupon the Tathāgata Viśeṣa placed his hand upon my head and said to me:
"You should level the ground of the mind; then all the grounds of the world will be level."
"Viśvabhū means 'pervading all with sovereignty.

He leveled the ground and path to await the Buddha's passage. The Buddha revealed the Dharma-gate of self-realization to cause him to level his mind; for when all things are made level, the mind is that upon which the myriad dharmas rely. It impartially nurtures and sustains all, and is therefore called 'ground' (bhūmi)."

If one can contemplate the nature of equality and remain in accord with it, then all phenomena are without exception equal; being sovereign and unimpeded, for this reason the Buddha is named "All-Sovereign."
2. Attaining Enlightenment through Instruction, in two parts:
1. Directly Stating the Essence of Enlightenment:

"My mind was immediately opened; I saw that the minute particles of my own body and all the minute particles that constitute the world are equal and without distinction. The self-nature of these particles does not touch one another; even weapons of war cannot touch them."

Upon hearing these words, his mind became level and he immediately realized that his own mind was fundamentally equal. He understood that all atoms within the body and the realms lack intrinsic nature; they manifest solely from false discrimination. There is but one true reality, the original Tathāgatagarbha, which is like a flower in the sky: it is seen falsely due to an optical impairment, yet the sky originally has no flowers—how, then, could there be any mutual obstruction?
For this reason, even the weapons of war could not touch him.
Second, through awakening he attained realization:

"I awakened to the patience of non-arising within the dharma-nature and became an arhat; now, having turned my mind, I enter the stage of a bodhisattva. Hearing the Tathāgatas proclaim the ground of the Buddhas' wondrous lotus-like knowledge and vision, I was first among those who testified to it and served as their leader."

The body-element and its two objects, as well as all phenomena of defilement and purity, are fundamentally without self-nature; they are solely the true mark, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, and are thus called the "dharma-nature.
To accept this with certainty—that it is originally devoid of arising and ceasing and is definitively unerring—is termed "the patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti).

As for this person who awakens to the Mahāyāna yet attains a fruit of the Hīnayāna, it is because he accords with their inclinations; if they require entry, he enters immediately. This is like the various Bodhisattvas of the Western Regions, all of whom realized the Great Way and regarded the Hīnayāna as something to be spat out, yet frequently attained the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle due to the invitations of kings. How could this not be so because of the inclinations of people?
In the past, Earth-Holding (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and beheld the "Universal Gate" chapter.
Second, he reiterated his conclusion as a response:

"When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I observed that the two objects—the body and the world—are equal and without distinction. Originally they are the Tathāgata-garbha; it is only through delusion that these objects arise. When the objects are dissolved, wisdom becomes perfect, and one achieves the Unsurpassed Way; this is the foremost."
This may be understood according to the text.
Third, the youth Candraprabha has three parts:
first, encountering the Buddha and receiving his teachings.
The youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I recall that in the past, as many eons ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Jaladeva. He taught various bodhisattvas to practice the contemplation of water and enter samādhi.”
"The moon is the yin essence and is able to produce water.
The names of the Buddhas encountered are all derived from their respective practices.
Second, cultivating contemplation according to the teachings, in two parts:"
I. A detailed exposition of the practice, in two parts:
A. The actual accomplishment of the perception of water, in two parts:
1. The actual cultivation of the perception.

"Observe that the watery element within the body cannot be displaced; it begins with mucus and saliva, and thus extends through all the fluids, essences, blood, feces, and urine. As these circulate and revolve within the body, the nature of their watery element is identical."
One sees that the water within one’s own body is no different from the fragrant oceans of the Floating Banner King lands outside the world-system.
Being of a single flavor as the element of water, it cannot be displaced by any other primary element; therefore, it is called "unassailable."

Regarding the Fragrant Water Ocean of the Floating Banner King World-system: according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the Flower Treasury Ocean there is a great lotus flower, and within that lotus flower are various fragrant water oceans; each of these fragrant water oceans serves as the seed for the world-systems of the Buddhas' lands. Now, observing that the water of one's own body is identical to those oceans, there is no distinction between them.
2. Narrating the Partial Realization:
"At that time, when I first accomplished this contemplation, I saw only the water and had not yet attained bodilessness.

When the perception of water was accomplished, I merely attained non-self; yet, because I still clung to the appearance of water as being entirely the body, the view of dharmas had not been extinguished, and thus I had not yet attained bodilessness.
2. Encountering Conditions through Contemplation, in four parts:
1. Encountering Conditions upon Entering Contemplation:
"While I was practicing dhyāna in my room as a bhikṣu, a disciple of mine peered through the window to observe the room; he saw nothing at all, except for clear water filling the entire room."
Being a young child without knowledge, he picked up a piece of tile or rubble and threw it into the water; as it struck the water and made a sound, he looked back and departed.
When he first formed this mental construct, although he saw that water as no different from the ocean of fragrant waters, it was merely what his own mind perceived and did not extend to others.

Now, as the power of meditative concentration becomes increasingly superior, the resultant form (*rūpa*) likewise becomes superior; it then becomes accessible to the vision of others, which is the actual fruit of true concentration. This differs from the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), where the perception is accomplished only within one's own vision.
2. Emerging from meditation as if ill:
"After emerging from samādhi, I suddenly felt pain in my heart, like that experienced by Śāriputra when he encountered the 'Harmful Ghost.
I reflected to myself:"

"I have now attained the path of Arhatship and have long been free from the conditions of illness; why is it that today I suddenly experience heart pain? Could it be that I am falling away from my realization?
Śāriputra entered meditative concentration on the banks of the Ganges and was seized by a ghost; upon emerging from concentration, he suffered a headache.
The Buddha said to him, "If you had not possessed meditative concentration, your body would have been shattered."
"Now I am likewise; I fear that I may fall away from the fruit of the path I have realized.
Third, he carefully examined the circumstances and pointed out the matter:
"At that time, the youth came quickly before me and spoke of the aforementioned events."
I then said to him:
"If you see water again, you may immediately open the door, enter this water, and remove the tiles and rubble.
Fourth, he attained peace through a second stabilization.
"The youth followed my instructions.
Later, when I entered meditative absorption, I again saw the water; the tiles and rubble were exactly as they were. I opened the door and cleared them out.
When I later emerged from absorption, my physical body was restored to its original state."
2. Realization through Cultivation:

"Having encountered immeasurable Buddhas, and continuing in this manner until reaching the Tathāgata Sovereign King of Mountains and Seas Supernatural Penetrations, he finally attained the dissolution of the self-body; thus, his nature merged with the true emptiness of the fragrant water-seas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, becoming non-dual and indistinguishable."
"Now, having attained the name 'Celibate Youth' (kumārabhūta) from the Tathāgata, you have joined the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

Previously, one still saw water; now, merging with true emptiness, there is no water to be found—all is the Tathāgatagarbha. Therefore, it is said that "the body perishes," which is to say one realizes the emptiness of dharmas.
3. Conclusion of the inquiry:
"The Buddha asked about perfect penetration; through the single flavor of the nature of water flowing everywhere, I attained the patience of non-arising and fulfilled Bodhi—this is the foremost."
4. Vimalaprabha Bodhisattva (Three Sections):
1. Encountering the Buddha and Receiving Instruction.
The Dharma Prince Vimalaprabha immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall that in the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Immeasurable Sound (*Amitaghoṣa*). He revealed to the bodhisattvas the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), observing that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all driven by the power of the winds of false conditions."
"Vaiḍūrya" is what it is called in its original language; this translates here as "jewel of the distant mountain.

Because one contemplates the wind-power that stirs one's own mind, and through the perfection of this contemplation attains its function, the body and mind become transparently clear like that vaidūrya gem; therefore, it is so named.
The Buddha encountered was named Immeasurable Sound (*Amitaghoṣa*), who likewise established his name by contemplating wind.

To contemplate wind as revealing original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*): wind is a characteristic of movement; since it belongs to the deluded, it is fundamentally without movement. That which is without movement is original enlightenment; thus, one contemplates movement in order to manifest that which is without movement.
2. Cultivating Contemplation Based on the Teachings, in two parts:
A. The Actual Practice of Contemplation.

"At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the realms, contemplated the movement of the world, contemplated the movement and stillness of the body, and contemplated the movement and thoughts of the mind; all movements were non-dual, equal and without distinction."
He identified the object of contemplation:

"I then realized that this nature of collective movement comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; the deluded sentient beings, as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, are all equally illusory. Thus it extends even to all sentient beings within a single world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds, like a hundred mosquitoes trapped in a single vessel, chirping and clamoring together, creating a frantic noise within a mere fraction of space."
This is correct observation.
Since both the world and the body-and-mind are all moved by wind, from where does the wind arise to move these things?
When things are not moving, where does it go?

Since the wind has no source, the movement of things is illusory; thus one perceives all sentient beings throughout the ten directions as wildly agitated by themselves, all equally false and fundamentally without cause.
2. Benefits Gained upon Accomplishing Contemplation.
"Not long after he had met the Buddha, he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, his mind opened and he beheld the land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the East. He became a Dharma Prince, serving the Buddhas of the ten directions; his body and mind emitted light, penetrating all things with unimpeded clarity."
Before long, it was as if it were still near at hand.
Relying on the instructions to observe, he realized the state of non-arising not long after receiving the teaching.
Because he observed arising and ceasing to realize the unarisen and undying, he beheld the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya in the eastern direction.

My own body and the vessel-world are both the original essence of fundamental enlightenment, wondrously luminous; therefore, it is said that "light is emitted, penetrating and transparent without obstruction.
Third, the conclusion answering the question:

"When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, I have realized the Bodhi-mind through observing that the power of wind has no dependence, thereby entering samādhi. This unifies me with the Buddhas of the ten directions and transmits this one wondrous mind; this is the foremost [method]."
5. The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja: Four sections.
First, that which is identical to what the Buddha has attained.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I and the Tathāgata have both attained the Boundless Body (ananta-kāya) from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
Dīpaṃkara is none other than the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.

Because he contemplated that the four great elements (mahābhūta) are falsely produced and that no substantial entity can be found, being identical to empty space, he attained a bodily form like empty space—pervasive and unimpeded.
2. A detailed account of the divine functions:
"At that time, he held four great precious jewels in his hands, which illuminated Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space."

Furthermore, within the great mirror manifested from my own mind, ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-light are emitted, flowing and permeating the banners and king-pinnacles of all lands throughout the ten directions to the very limits of empty space; these enter into the mirror and penetrate my body.

"The body is identical to empty space and does not obstruct one another; the body is able to skillfully enter lands as small as motes of dust, extensively performing Buddha-works, and attaining great accordance.

Contemplating the nature of the four great elements and one's own mind, one finds them to be nothing but perfectly bright and pure precious awareness. The essence of this awareness is unobstructed and pervades all things; therefore, it can use the four precious jewels to illuminate the worlds of the ten directions, transforming them into empty space.

Within the mirror manifested in the mind, light illuminates all lands; these enter into the mirror, such that bodies and lands mutually penetrate one another without mutual obstruction, performing buddha-works in vast accordance with reality.
The ten kinds of light refer to the ten bodies of Vairocana.
Third, realization is attained through contemplation:

"This great supernatural power arises from my profound contemplation that the four elements have no basis, that false thoughts arise and perish, and that empty space is non-dual; that the Buddha-lands are fundamentally identical. By illuminating this identity, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
This describes the attainment of patience through the perfection of contemplation, giving rise to this great function.
The four elements, body and mind, empty space, and the Buddha-lands are all equally illusory; they are solely the perfect and eternal.
This profound manifestation of function is not constrained by spatial location.
Fourth, the conclusion that answers the question:
"The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; I have entered samādhi by contemplating the boundlessness of space, whereby my wondrous power is perfectly clear and bright—this is the foremost."
"Because he contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), his body and his land manifest in mutual interpenetration; it is on this basis that he receives the name 'Gaganagañja' (Space-Treasury).
Sixth, Maitreya Bodhisattva, in three parts:
1. Meeting the Buddha and receiving his teachings."
Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I recall that in the past, after the passage of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa.”
I received the going-forth from that Buddha, yet my mind placed great weight on worldly fame, and I delighted in visiting the families of the nobility.
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to practice the samādhi of consciousness-only and enter into samāpatti.
His full name is Maitreya; in this language, it means "Kindly One" (Cishi).
During the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was one among the eight hundred disciples of the Bodhisattva Prabhāpāla who was named Yaśaskāma; he is this very person.

Those whose minds value worldly fame and frequent the families of the noble are generally led by their perception of objects external to the mind; they pursue them without ceasing, discriminating among the various categories, names, and characteristics of phenomena. Not knowing that these are manifestations produced by the habitual perfuming of one's own mind, they fail to understand the mind and its conditions, thereby giving rise to two kinds of deluded conceptions.
To serve as an antidote, the meditation on consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is taught.
Second, the cultivation of meditation based on the teachings has two parts:
first, long-term cultivation that eliminates faults.
"Throughout kalpas past, I have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges by means of this samādhi; my pursuit of worldly fame and reputation has ceased and vanished.

When first practicing this contemplation, one attains the remedial power [of insight], knowing that worldly fame and profit—whether existent or non-existent, abundant or meager—are all transformations of one's own *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and do not come from elsewhere; consequently, the frantic pursuit of them is suddenly brought to rest.
2. Attaining the Way through the Perfection of Contemplation, in two parts:
1. Realizing Mind-Only:

"From the time Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world until now, I have attained the unsurpassed, wondrous, and perfect Samādhi of the Consciousness-Mind; even all the lands of the Tathāgatas throughout the entirety of space—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—are all manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind."
When this contemplation is first accomplished, its stage corresponds to that of "practice through understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*).
Now, having attained samādhi and correctly entered the first bhūmi, it is called the "True Path of Seeing" (*darśana-mārga*).

This means that the single, ultimate, fundamental non-conceptual wisdom merges in profound harmony with the *dharmadhātu*; subject and object are of one suchness, without two distinct characteristics. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* verse says: "When, regarding the object of cognition, the wisdom perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in *vijñaptimātra*, because one is free from the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper."

At that time, it is precisely called "direct realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*); even unto the exhaustion of the Tathāgata’s lands—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—all are manifested as transformations of my own mind. Therefore, among the five stages, this is termed the "stage of penetration" (*prativedha-avasthā*).
2. Manifesting All Buddhas.
“World-Honored One!

Because I have realized that all is but mind-consciousness, the nature of consciousness has flowed forth as immeasurable Tathāgatas; I have now received the prediction that I shall next succeed to the seat of Buddhahood.”

Since one is already able to manifest the direct realization of the true principle of Consciousness-Only—that both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the pure and the impure, are all manifestations of the mind alone—innumerable Buddhas flow forth from the nature of consciousness.
That I have now attained this succession to the Buddha is likewise a transformation of my own consciousness and not due to anything else.
Third, reiterating the conclusion of the response:

"When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I observed with clarity that the ten directions are mere consciousness. As the mind of consciousness became perfectly luminous, I entered the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), remaining far removed from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Thus I attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is the foremost."

First, one contemplates that both the defiled and the pure, as well as the primary and secondary realms, are all transformations of consciousness alone; since they originally lack intrinsic nature, one does not give rise to false and pervasive attachments that conceive of a self or phenomena, thereby departing from the parikalpita-svabhāva (the imagined nature).

It is decisively understood that both the subject that transforms and the object that is transformed are fundamentally the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous nature of Bodhi; they are thus detached from the *paratantra* (dependent nature) and are solely the perfectly accomplished (*pariniṣpanna*) and pure jewel-like awakening. Therefore, it is said that one is far removed from both the *paratantra* and the *parikalpita* (imagined) attachments.

Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The first is the naturelessness of characteristics; the second is the absence of intrinsic nature; and the last is due to being far removed from the previously grasped natures of self and phenomena."
This is precisely that meaning.
Seven: Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, in three parts:
first, encountering the Buddha and receiving his teachings.
2. First, the introduction:
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Dharma Prince, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall that in the past, as many kalpas ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Immeasurable Light. Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another during that single kalpa, the last of whom was named Surpassing the Sun and Moon."
"That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
It is also called "Attaining Great Power through Immeasurable Light," as explained in the *Contemplation Sūtra*.
The Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha will be clarified below.
2. Exposition of the Teaching, in two parts:
1. Illustration by analogy, in two parts:
1. Illustration of the fault of non-remembrance.

"It is like, for example, one person who is single-mindedly intent on mindfulness and another who is single-mindedly intent on delusion; such two people may meet and yet not meet, or see and yet not see.
Single-minded mindfulness is like the Buddha; single-minded forgetfulness refers to those who do not practice recollection.
Thus, because sentient beings' visions of the Buddha are not fixed, it is said that "whether they meet him or not," and so forth.
Second is the analogy for attaining the mindfulness of the Buddha:
"Two people think of one another; their mutual remembrance is deep. Thus, from birth to birth, they are like a form and its shadow, never becoming separated."
Because the Buddha and sentient beings are in accord through mindfulness, the Buddha and sentient beings are like a form and its shadow.
Second, the correspondence of dharmas, in two parts:
first, the correspondence of non-mindfulness.
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child; if the child has run away, what can mere remembrance accomplish?
To remember them like a mother is the Buddha.
If a son has fled and gone away, he is still alive;
though one may remember him, what is the use? For they will not meet again.
Second, the combined mindfulness of the Buddha, which has two parts:
1. The Analogy of Mutual Remembrance:
"If a child remembers its mother as much as the mother remembers the child, then throughout successive lives, mother and child will not be separated or far apart.

If sentient beings remember the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name with their minds, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future; they will not be far from the Buddha, and without relying on expedient means, they will naturally attain the opening of the mind."
First, the primary parable: if the assembly is already in close proximity, there is no need for them to descend to receive benefit.
Second, the parable used to further clarify:
"Just as a person who has been anointed with incense has a fragrance upon their body, this is called the Adornment of Fragrant Light."
As incense that is perfumed possesses fragrance, so by recollecting the Buddha one attains the vision of the Buddha; cause and effect correspond to one another—who would say otherwise?
Second, through cultivation, realization is attained.

"I originally attained the stage of non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by means of the mind that recollects the Buddha; now, within this world-system, I gather those who recollect the Buddha and lead them back to the Pure Land. Regarding "recollecting the Buddha to enter non-arising":

at the outset, one uses the mind of arising and ceasing to take the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Buddha as its object, focusing single-mindedly on this one realm without interruption. One beholds the Buddha’s marks and signs, his radiant adornments, his environment (*niśraya*), his retinue, and each of his joyful activities, as if looking at one's own face in a clear mirror; surveying everything with wide-open eyes, there is nothing that is not the fruition of Buddhahood.
Thereafter, one further contemplates that all realms associated with the Buddha whom one is mindful of are collectively illusory and lack inherent nature from the outset.
Since they manifest solely from the activity of thought, from where could the mind that is capable of mindfulness—whether already arisen or yet to arise—possibly exist?
Not perceiving a single dharma, it is ultimately empty and quiescent.

Because the mind does not perceive the mind, no characteristic can be apprehended; thus, both subject and object are simultaneously stilled. Being fundamentally free from thought, that which is free from the characteristics of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception. This single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharmakāya.

This means that by recollecting the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), one perceives the Dharma-body Buddha, which is precisely the thought of non-arising; therefore, it is said that "by the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, one enters the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

Since I have already attained deliverance, the Dharma-body of sentient beings is no different from my own. Because this non-differentiated nature mutually interpenetrates, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are all gathered by me; thus, it is said that "those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are brought back to the Pure Land."
3. Conclusion and Response to the Question:

“When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, I have no preference; by universally withdrawing the six sense organs and maintaining a continuous flow of pure mindfulness, I attained samādhi—this is the foremost.”
"Mindfulness belongs to the faculty of mind; since the faculty of mind is that upon which all faculties rely, it encompasses the six.
Mindfulness is itself non-mindfulness, hence it is called 'pure mindfulness.
Because there is no interruption by [other] thoughts, it is called 'continuous.'"
This is precisely the entry into the nature of the faculties and the great elements.
*Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle Five, Part Two.
